paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Magnetism is the group of physical effects that happen through a magnetic field, which lets objects attract or repel each other. Both electric currents and the magnetic moments of elementary particles create magnetic fields, so magnetism is one of the two sides of electromagnetism. Away from a local magnetic source, the field weakens with distance. An object's field depends on many things, including the magnetic moment of its material, its shape, any electric current inside it, and its temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Strong and weak magnetism
paragraphs.text: The familiar effects come from ferromagnetic materials. These are strongly attracted to magnetic fields and can be magnetized into permanent magnets that make fields of their own. Only a few substances are ferromagnetic, most commonly iron, cobalt, nickel and their alloys. Yet every substance shows some kind of magnetism. Paramagnetic ones such as aluminium and oxygen are weakly attracted, diamagnetic ones such as copper and carbon are weakly repelled, and antiferromagnetic ones such as chromium respond in a more complex way; their forces are usually too weak to feel, so they are often called non-magnetic.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient lodestones
paragraphs.text: People first noticed magnetism when lodestones, naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite, pulled on iron. The word magnet comes from a Greek phrase meaning the Magnesian stone, or lodestone. Aristotle credited Thales of Miletus with the first discussion of magnetism that could be called scientific. In India, the medical text Sushruta Samhita describes using magnetite to draw out arrows stuck in a person's body.

paragraphs.heading: Compasses and treatises
paragraphs.text: By the 12th century the Chinese used lodestone compasses for navigation, carving a spoon from lodestone so that its handle always pointed south. By 1187 Alexander Neckam had described the compass and its use for finding the way, the first person in Europe to do so. The oldest treatise on magnets that still survives is the Epistola de magnete, written by Peter Peregrinus de Maricourt in 1269. In 1600 William Gilbert published De Magnete, concluding from experiments with a model Earth, the terrella, that the Earth itself is magnetic and that this is why compasses point north.

paragraphs.heading: Electricity joins in
paragraphs.text: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted saw a compass needle twitch near a wire by accident and realised an electric current could make a magnetic field. That same year Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart gave an equation for the field around a wire carrying current. André-Marie Ampère, around the same time, ran careful experiments on the force between loops of current. In 1831 Michael Faraday found that a magnetic flux changing over time induces a voltage in a wire loop.

paragraphs.heading: One theory
paragraphs.text: In 1835 Carl Friedrich Gauss proposed that all magnetism comes from elementary point charges moving relative to each other. From around 1861 James Clerk Maxwell drew these ideas together into Maxwell's equations, uniting electricity, magnetism and optics as electromagnetism. In 1905 Albert Einstein used those equations to motivate special relativity, which demands that the laws hold in every inertial frame. Electromagnetism has kept growing since, becoming part of quantum electrodynamics, electroweak theory and the Standard Model.
